facts.statement: Aletopelta is estimated to have been 5 meters long and weighed 2 tonnes.
facts.quote: Aletopelta has an estimated size of 5 metres (16 feet) and weight of 2 tonnes (4,409 lbs).

facts.statement: The holotype skeleton was discovered in 1987 during construction work near Carlsbad, California, where a ditch for a sewage pipe uncovered the remains.
facts.quote: In 1987, construction work was done on the College Boulevard near Carlsbad at the Californian coast. While paleontologically surveying the work, Bradford Riney noted that a skeleton had been uncovered by a ditch dug for a sewage pipe.

facts.statement: The skeleton was first described in 1996 by Deméré and Coombs and formally named in 2001 by Ford and Kirkland.
facts.quote: The skeleton was later described, but not named, in 1996 by Thomas Deméré and Walter Preston Coombs before being named in 2001 by Tracy Lee Ford and James Kirkland.

facts.statement: The holotype carcass was washed into the sea, sank upside down, and became a miniature reef inhabited by marine invertebrates.
facts.quote: The type and only known specimen of Aletopelta was once a bloated carcass that had been washed out to sea, likely by a stream, which sank to the bottom with its underside facing upwards and became a miniature reef, as evidence by Pelecypoda such as Ostrea sp. and Spondylus sp. being attached to the bones and the presence of ammonites and gastropods found in association with the skeleton.

facts.statement: Sharks and marine invertebrates scavenged the carcass, leaving hollow long bones and pits on the armor.
facts.quote: The carcass was also scavenged upon by marine invertebrates and sharks such as Squalicorax and Scapanorhynchus, which resulted with most of the long bones being hollow and many shallow pits on the osteoderms and ribs.

facts.statement: While originally estimated at 6 meters long, Gregory S. Paul later estimated the length at 5 meters and weight at 2 tonnes.
facts.quote: Ford & Kirkland (2001) originally gave Aletopelta an estimated length of 6 metres (19.7 feet). However, Gregory S. Paul gave a lower estimate of 5 metres (16 feet) long and weight of 2 tonnes (4,409 lbs) in 2010.

facts.statement: Aletopelta is characterized by wide teeth, a femur longer than the tibia and fibula, three metatarsals, a polygonal pelvic shield, shoulder spikes, and various hollow osteoderms.
facts.quote: Ford and Kirkland (2001) originally diagnosed Aletopelta based on the teeth being wider than tall; the femur being much longer than both the tibia and fibula; the presence of three metatarsals; a pelvic shield composed of polygonal, low-peaked osteoderms; a large short-pointed spike in the shoulder region; the presence of hollow cap-like osteoderms across dorsum; the presence of hollow pup-tent-like osteoderms over neck and shoulders; triangular, dorsally compressed caudal osteoderms that are highly asymmetrical from top to bottom; and hollow and thin osteoderms.

facts.statement: Arbour and Currie (2015) diagnosed the genus based on hexagonal pelvic osteoderms forming a semi-continuous sheet and a specific fusion pattern in the neck armor.
facts.quote: However, Arbour & Currie (2015) later diagnosed Aletopelta based on the presence of hexagonal pelvic osteoderms that form a semi-continuous sheet over the pelvis; the pelvic osteoderms lack a dendritic surface texture; the first cervical half ring is composed of osteoderms fused to an underlying bony band rather than being closely appressed adjacent osteoderms.

facts.statement: Ford and Kirkland (2001) classified Aletopelta as a distinct genus and species within the family Ankylosauridae.
facts.quote: Ford & Kirkland (2001) also reinterpreted it as an ankylosaurid and considered it to be taxonomically distinct enough to be warranted as a new genus and species.

facts.statement: Vickaryous et al. (2004) considered Aletopelta a nomen dubium due to insufficient diagnostic features.
facts.quote: Vickaryous et al. (2004) considered Aletopelta as a nomen dubium due to the lack of diagnostic characteristics.

facts.statement: Arbour and Currie (2015) argued for the validity of the genus based on new characteristics and rejected the subfamily Stegopeltinae.
facts.quote: Arbour & Currie (2015), however, considered it as a valid genus based on new characteristics and found Stegopeltinae to not be a valid clade.

facts.statement: While often placed as a basal ankylosaurid, some studies suggest it may be the most basal nodosaurid.
facts.quote: Although most often being recovered as a basal ankylosaurid, Frauenfelder et al. (2022) found it to be the basalmost nodosaurid.

facts.statement: The fossil record for Aletopelta spans from 83.6 to 72.2 million years ago.
facts.quote: Time range: Campanian to Campanian (83.6 to 72.2 million years ago)

facts.statement: Kirkland and Ford placed Aletopelta in the family Ankylosauridae rather than Nodosauridae based on its unique armor arrangement.
facts.quote: Aletopelta es colocado por Kirkland y Ford dentro de la familia Ankylosauridae y no en Nodosauridae como en los primeros informes, debido al arreglo particular de la armadura.

facts.statement: The holotype specimen includes a femur that is much longer than the tibia and ulna, along with three metatarsals.
facts.quote: El holotipo, SDNHM 33909, consta de un fémur que es mucho más largo que la tibia y la ulna y tenía 3 metatarsianos.

facts.statement: The armor consists of shoulder spikes and shields, low keeled plates on the sides, and a mosaic of small polygonal osteoderms at the hip level.
facts.quote: La armadura consiste en espinas y escudos en los hombros, a los lados placas bajas con forma de quilla y un mosaico de pequeños osículos de forma poligonal a la altura de la cadera.

rejected.statement: Aletopelta is a monospecific genus of basal ankylosaurid dinosaur that lived in Southern California during the Late Cretaceous.
rejected.quote: Aletopelta (; meaning 'wanderer shield') is a monospecific genus of basal ankylosaurid dinosaur from Southern California that lived during the Late Cretaceous (upper Campanian stage, 75.5 Ma) in what is now the Point Loma Formation.
